triage.name: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
triage.reason: Family history, flank pain, hematuria and hypertension with characteristic imaging; a strong genetics and nephrology case with clear diagnostic criteria.

demographics: Affects all ethnic groups; occurs worldwide
Accounts for a substantial share of adults with end-stage kidney disease
Often diagnosed in adulthood, though cysts begin forming in childhood

risk_factors.text: Family history of polycystic kidney disease in a parent
Known pathogenic PKD1 or PKD2 variant in the family
Age over 30 with an affected parent

family_history: Polycystic kidney disease in a parent
Kidney failure or dialysis in a relative
Early stroke or brain aneurysm in a relative

chief_complaints.text: My blood pressure has been high
I feel a fullness or lump in my belly
I'm tired and my legs are swollen

hpi.onset: Gradual, often noticed in the 30s to 40s; many people have no symptoms until cysts enlarge or kidney function declines
hpi.duration: Months to years of intermittent symptoms before diagnosis
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; flank discomfort and abdominal fullness increase as cysts grow, and kidney function gradually declines over decades
hpi.location: Flank and back, often bilateral; abdominal fullness is diffuse
hpi.radiation: Flank pain may radiate to the groin or lower abdomen
hpi.quality: Dull, aching, or pressure-like; can become sharp and severe during cyst hemorrhage or stone passage
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate most days, with episodes of severe pain during bleeding into a cyst or a kidney stone
hpi.timing: Intermittent, worse with activity or jarring; hematuria may be episodic
pertinent_negatives: Painless gross hematuria with no family history
Recent strep throat or skin infection followed by dark urine
Flank pain with fever and chills suggesting acute pyelonephritis
Weight loss, night sweats, or fever suggesting malignancy or infection
Exposure to nephrotoxic drugs or contrast dye

atypical.how_it_differs: Children are usually asymptomatic; cysts may be seen on imaging done for other reasons, and hypertension or gross hematuria can be the first sign.
Present with advanced kidney disease, anemia, and more prominent liver cysts; pain may be less prominent than fatigue and uremic symptoms.
Enlarged kidneys and hypertension increase the risk of preeclampsia and preterm delivery; pain may be attributed to pregnancy.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort, able to lie flat, no toxic appearance
general.severe: Ill-appearing, uncomfortable, prefers not to move

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen bimanually in both flanks
findings.finding: Enlarged, irregular, nodular kidneys palpable bilaterally

findings.maneuver: Palpate the costovertebral angles and flanks
Palpate the liver edge below the right costal margin
findings.finding: Enlarged liver with a nodular or irregular edge

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms with an appropriately sized cuff
Press the dorsum of each foot and the pretibial area
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the cardiac apex and left sternal border
findings.finding: Mid-systolic click or late systolic murmur of mitral valve prolapse

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam including cranial nerves, strength and coordination
Inspect the jugular venous pulse at 45 degrees

labs.caveat: Creatinine rises only after substantial nephron loss; a normal value does not exclude significant cystic disease.
Metabolic acidosis from declining kidney function.
Hyperkalemia appears with advanced kidney failure; watch closely if on ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
Normocytic anemia of chronic kidney disease; may also drop acutely with cyst hemorrhage.
Hematuria may be microscopic between episodes of gross bleeding.
Proteinuria is usually mild; heavy proteinuria suggests a different glomerular disease.
Sterile pyuria can occur with cyst infection or a stone; correlate with culture.
Hyperuricemia and gout are more common as kidney function declines.
Rises with cyst infection or pyelonephritis; not specific.
Leukocytosis suggests infected cyst or pyelonephritis rather than uncomplicated disease.

findings.finding: Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria from chronic hypertension
Nonspecific ST-T changes from left ventricular hypertrophy

imaging.preferred_when: First-line screening and diagnosis, especially in younger patients and pregnancy

findings.text: Multiple bilateral renal cysts of varying size
Enlarged kidneys with increased total kidney volume
Increased echogenicity of the renal parenchyma

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When ultrasound is nondiagnostic or complications such as hemorrhage, stone or cyst infection are suspected

findings.text: Numerous bilateral renal cysts with enlarged kidneys

imaging.study: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When precise cyst and kidney volume measurement is needed, or CT is contraindicated

findings.text: Multiple bilateral renal cysts with measurable total kidney volume
Cyst hemorrhage with high signal on T1-weighted images

imaging.study: CT angiography or MR angiography of the brain
imaging.preferred_when: Screening for intracranial aneurysm in patients with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage
When a murmur or symptoms suggest valvular disease

initial.why: Assesses kidney function, electrolytes and acid-base status
Looks for anemia of chronic kidney disease and leukocytosis suggesting infection
First-line imaging to show bilateral cysts and enlarged kidneys
Hyperuricemia and gout are associated with progressive disease
Rules out pregnancy before imaging and guides management
initial.only_if: patient is a woman of childbearing age

confirmatory.test: CT abdomen and pelvis without IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Confirms cyst burden and evaluates complications when ultrasound is nondiagnostic

confirmatory.test: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
confirmatory.why: Accurate cyst and total kidney volume measurement when needed

supporting.why: Supports suspicion of infected cyst or pyelonephritis
supporting.only_if: fever or flank pain suggests infection

supporting.test: CT angiography or MR angiography of the brain
supporting.only_if: family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage

supporting.why: Evaluates mitral valve prolapse or left ventricular hypertrophy

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Contrast risks kidney injury; noncontrast imaging is preferred unless another diagnosis requires it
Not needed when imaging and family history are diagnostic and carries bleeding risk from cysts
Reserved for equivocal imaging, young patients with no family history, or family planning; not routine

not_indicated.test: CT angiography or MR angiography of the brain
not_indicated.why: Not routine without a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage

decision_points: Use age-specific ultrasound cyst counts to make the diagnosis in patients with a positive family history
Screen for intracranial aneurysm only when there is a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs and NSAIDs; control blood pressure to slow progression
Pregnancy test before imaging in anyone who could be pregnant

criteria.name: Ultrasound diagnostic criteria for ADPKD in at-risk individuals
criteria.summary: In a person with a family history, the number of renal cysts needed for diagnosis depends on age: at least 3 cysts total in those under 30, at least 2 cysts in each kidney at ages 30 to 39, and at least 4 cysts in each kidney at age 40 or older. Imaging findings are combined with family history and, when needed, genetic testing.

differential.name: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
differential.why_considered: Multiple bilateral renal cysts in a young patient with enlarged kidneys and reduced kidney function
differential.trigger: Cystic kidneys in an infant or young child, or a patient with congenital hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension

history: Cysts and kidney failure present in infancy or early childhood
Parents are unaffected and often consanguineous
History of portal hypertension or variceal bleeding
exam: Growth failure and failure to thrive
Signs of portal hypertension such as splenomegaly or ascites
labs: Reduced kidney function from a young age
Elevated liver enzymes or evidence of synthetic liver dysfunction
imaging: Diffusely echogenic enlarged kidneys with radially oriented microcysts rather than discrete macrocysts
Liver fibrosis with a normal biliary tree on MR cholangiopancreatography

differential.name: Simple renal cysts
differential.why_considered: One or more renal cysts found on imaging during a workup for flank pain or hematuria

history: No family history of polycystic kidney disease
Older age, typically over 50
No childhood or early adult symptoms
imaging: One or a few cysts, often unilateral

differential.name: Von Hippel-Lindau disease
differential.why_considered: Multiple renal cysts in a young patient with a family history of kidney disease
differential.trigger: Renal cysts plus retinal angiomas, cerebellar hemangioblastomas, or pheochromocytoma

history: Visual disturbance or retinal lesions
Headaches, ataxia, or other cerebellar symptoms
Episodes of palpitations, sweating, and hypertension suggesting pheochromocytoma
exam: Cerebellar signs or focal neurologic deficits
Signs of catecholamine excess such as tachycardia and diaphoresis
labs: Normal kidney function early in the disease
imaging: Renal cysts and solid renal tumors (clear cell carcinoma)

differential.name: Tuberous sclerosis complex
differential.why_considered: Multiple renal cysts and kidney enlargement in a patient with a genetic syndrome

history: Infantile spasms or seizures
Developmental delay or intellectual disability
Hypopigmented skin patches since birth
exam: Ash-leaf spots, shagreen patches, or facial angiofibromas
labs: Genetic testing showing TSC1 or TSC2 variants
imaging: Cortical tubers and subependymal nodules on brain MRI

differential.name: Medullary cystic kidney disease
differential.why_considered: Cystic kidney disease with progressive kidney failure and a family history

history: Kidney failure developing in adulthood with minimal hypertension early on
Family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance but no flank pain or hematuria
No liver cysts
labs: Progressive kidney failure with early anemia
imaging: Cysts confined to the medulla or corticomedullary junction

differential.name: Acquired cystic kidney disease
differential.why_considered: Multiple bilateral renal cysts in a patient with chronic kidney disease

history: Long-standing kidney failure, often on dialysis for years
No family history of polycystic kidney disease
No childhood or early adult cystic disease
exam: Small, shrunken kidneys rather than enlarged ones
Signs of end-stage kidney disease such as uremic fetor or volume overload
labs: Severe kidney failure with elevated creatinine and anemia
No hematuria unless a cyst bleeds
imaging: Small kidneys with multiple cysts in the cortex and medulla
Possible renal cell carcinoma arising in a cyst

differential.name: Urinary tract obstruction with hydronephrosis
differential.why_considered: Flank pain, hematuria, and enlarged kidneys on imaging

history: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
History of kidney stones or prior obstruction
No family history of polycystic kidney disease
labs: Kidney function may be normal or acutely reduced
imaging: Dilated renal pelvis and calyces with a normal parenchyma
No multiple cysts replacing the parenchyma

differential.name: Glomerulonephritis
differential.why_considered: Hematuria, hypertension, and reduced kidney function in a young adult

history: Recent upper respiratory or skin infection
Dark or cola-colored urine
No family history of cystic kidney disease
labs: Active urinary sediment with red blood cell casts and dysmorphic red blood cells
Proteinuria, sometimes in the nephrotic range
Low complement levels in post-infectious glomerulonephritis
imaging: Normal or increased echogenicity without discrete cysts

severity.mild: Normal or near-normal kidney function with a few cysts, mild or no hypertension, and no pain or hematuria; often found through family screening
severity.moderate: Enlarged palpable kidneys, hypertension requiring treatment, intermittent flank pain or hematuria, and mild to moderate reduction in kidney function
severity.severe: Marked kidney enlargement with chronic pain, recurrent cyst hemorrhage or stones, and advanced chronic kidney disease with anemia and metabolic complications
severity.critical: End-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplantation, or a life-threatening complication such as ruptured intracranial aneurysm, infected cyst with sepsis, or severe hemorrhage

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe headache with neck stiffness, vomiting, or loss of consciousness
red_flags.meaning: Ruptured intracranial aneurysm with subarachnoid hemorrhage; needs emergency imaging and neurosurgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Fever with flank pain and rigors in a patient with known cysts
red_flags.meaning: Infected cyst or pyelonephritis; may require prolonged antibiotics and drainage

red_flags.finding: Gross hematuria with hypotension or a falling hemoglobin
red_flags.meaning: Significant cyst hemorrhage; assess hemodynamic status and transfusion needs
Obstruction from a stone or clot, or acute kidney injury; needs urgent imaging and relief of obstruction

red_flags.finding: Severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs
red_flags.meaning: Cyst rupture or another acute abdominal process; surgical evaluation required

complications.name: Hypertension
clues: Elevated blood pressure at routine visits
Left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG or echocardiogram

complications.name: Nephrolithiasis
clues: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin

complications.name: Urinary tract infection and infected cyst
clues: Pyuria with or without positive urine culture

complications.name: Chronic kidney disease and end-stage kidney disease
Intracranial aneurysm and subarachnoid hemorrhage
clues: Family history of aneurysm or early stroke

complications.name: Liver cysts and polycystic liver disease
Mitral valve prolapse
clues: Mid-systolic click or late systolic murmur

special_populations.differences: Usually asymptomatic; cysts may be found incidentally, and hypertension or gross hematuria can be the first sign. Diagnosis relies on age-specific cyst counts on ultrasound.
More likely to present with advanced kidney disease, anemia, and prominent liver cysts; pain may be less prominent than fatigue and uremic symptoms.
Enlarged kidneys and hypertension increase the risk of preeclampsia and preterm delivery; blood pressure control must be adjusted, and ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated.
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs and NSAIDs; adjust medication doses for kidney function and monitor electrolytes closely, especially potassium with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have polycystic kidney disease, kidney failure, or need dialysis?
key_questions.looking_for: A parent or relative with polycystic kidney disease or kidney failure; autosomal dominant inheritance means an affected parent in most cases

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have cysts in your kidneys or liver?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior imaging showing renal or hepatic cysts, or a known diagnosis in a relative prompting screening

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and what does it feel like?
key_questions.looking_for: Dull, aching flank or back pain, often bilateral, worse with activity or jarring; sudden severe pain suggests cyst hemorrhage or a stone

key_questions.question: Have you noticed blood in your urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Episodic gross hematuria or microscopic hematuria; may follow cyst rupture or stone passage

key_questions.question: Have you had your blood pressure checked, and has it been high?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypertension, often the earliest manifestation and a major driver of progression

key_questions.question: Have you had kidney stones or a urinary tract infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent stones or infections, which are common complications of cystic kidneys

key_questions.question: Have you felt a fullness or lump in your abdomen?
key_questions.looking_for: Abdominal distension from enlarged kidneys or liver cysts

key_questions.question: Are you more tired than usual, or have your legs been swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Fatigue, anemia, or edema suggesting declining kidney function

key_questions.question: Have you had sudden severe headaches, vision changes, or a family member with a brain aneurysm or early stroke?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of intracranial aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage, which guides screening

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including over-the-counter pain relievers?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAID use or other nephrotoxins that can worsen kidney function; ACE inhibitors or ARBs for blood pressure and kidney protection

key_questions.question: Do you have any children, or are you planning a family?
key_questions.looking_for: Interest in genetic counseling and family screening, since each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the condition

reasoning_points: Family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance, often an affected parent
Bilateral enlarged, nodular kidneys with multiple cysts on imaging
Hypertension, flank pain, and episodic hematuria in an adult
Age-specific ultrasound cyst counts in an at-risk individual support the diagnosis
Extrarenal findings such as liver cysts, intracranial aneurysm, or mitral valve prolapse
Alternative cystic and glomerular diseases considered and excluded

easy: Adult with a parent who has polycystic kidney disease
Hypertension with flank pain and hematuria
Ultrasound showing multiple bilateral renal cysts
medium: Young adult with hypertension and only microscopic hematuria
Incidental liver cysts leading to renal imaging
Normal kidney function despite enlarged cystic kidneys
hard: Child or adolescent with few cysts and no symptoms
Patient presenting with complications such as infected cyst, stone, or subarachnoid hemorrhage
No known family history, mimicking simple cysts or acquired cystic disease
Advanced kidney failure where kidneys are no longer clearly enlarged
